analysis.one_liner: Taxes trades of stocks, bonds, and derivatives to fund public investments, shielding small investors.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced in May 2015 with one cosponsor, referred to the Senate Finance Committee, and never received a hearing, a markup, or a vote before the Congress ended in January 2017.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would put a small tax on every trade of stocks, bonds, and derivatives — 0.5% on stock transfers, 0.1% on bonds, and 0.005% on derivatives. Large trading firms that buy and sell thousands of times a second would pay the most. Households making under $50,000 ($75,000 for couples) would get the tax back as a credit, so small savers and retirement accounts would be spared. The bill's findings say the money would go to free college, child care, infrastructure, health programs, and climate resilience.
analysis.who_benefits: Low- and moderate-income households, who get a full credit for any tax they pay, and the public programs the revenue is directed toward: free college, expanded child care, infrastructure repair, and health spending. Slow, long-term investors pay little; heavy speculative traders pay the most.

how_it_helps.text: Imposes an excise tax of 0.5% on stock transfers, 0.1% on bonds, and 0.005% on derivatives, paid by the exchange, broker, or trader [S3].
Gives a full tax credit to individuals with modified adjusted gross income up to $50,000 ($75,000 joint), indexed to inflation, so most ordinary savers get any tax they paid back [S3].
States the revenue would fund free college, student debt relief, child care, Social Security, infrastructure and green jobs, housing assistance, and international health programs [S3].
Its findings argue the tax would curb high-frequency trading, which it says may be up to 70% of the market and adds volatility, and notes the U.S. had a similar transfer tax from 1914 to 1966 [S3].

analysis.who_pays: High-frequency trading firms, Wall Street banks, hedge funds, and other heavy traders, who would pay the tax on every transaction. Exchanges and brokers bear collection duties. Some portion of the tax could reach ordinary investors indirectly through slightly higher trading costs, which the credit would offset only below the income limits.
analysis.who_pays_short: Wall Street banks and rapid-fire trading firms

drawbacks.text: Critics of transaction taxes generally argue trades migrate to foreign venues, trading costs rise somewhat, and market liquidity falls; the bill tries to address the first by taxing any purchase where a party is a U.S. person and empowering the Treasury Secretary to write anti-avoidance rules [S3].

The tax would raise costs for some investors above the income thresholds — including middle-class retirement accounts — since the credit phases out entirely at $50,000 individual / $75,000 joint income [S3].

The bill never specified where the revenue would legally go — it states findings about intended uses but does not actually appropriate funds to any program, so the tax and the spending were not linked in the legislation itself [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The tax is genuinely progressive: the heaviest traders pay the most, small households get every dollar back, and short-term debt under 60 days and municipal bonds are exempt. The main honest objections are that part of the cost can leak to ordinary investors above the income cutoffs, that trading could shift abroad despite the anti-avoidance rules, and that the bill is a statement of priorities more than a finished law — the revenue is never actually appropriated to the programs it names.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Finance Committee on the day it was introduced, and the committee never held a hearing or vote, so it died when the 114th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Introduced May 19, 2015 by Sen. Sanders with Sen. Schatz as cosponsor [S1] [S4].
Read twice and referred to the Committee on Finance the same day; no further action was ever taken [S5].
The bill expired at the end of the 114th Congress on January 3, 2017, without a hearing, a committee vote, or a floor vote [S5] [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Wall Street trading firms and banks, which avoided a tax on their transactions, and the Finance Committee leadership, which never had to take a position on it. No public program gained funding.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: High-volume trading firms on Wall Street

for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill as its only additional supporter

against.name: Orrin Hatch
against.what_they_did: As chair of the committee to which the bill was referred, never scheduled a hearing or markup; the bill shows no committee action for the rest of the Congress

against.name: Mitch McConnell
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to the Senate floor at any point in the 114th Congress

sides.party_line_note: The bill had no committee or floor vote, so no party breakdown exists in the record; its only two supporters were an independent and one Democrat, and the Republican-run Finance Committee and Senate majority never acted on it.

industries.industry: High-frequency and other high-volume trading firms
industries.note: They would pay the tax on every transaction and gain nothing from the spending, so their interest runs against the bill's public purpose. The bill's findings argue these firms make up to 70% of trading volume while adding volatility [S3].

industries.industry: Wall Street banks and securities dealers
industries.note: They would pay the tax on stock, bond, and derivative transactions and bear collection responsibilities, while the revenue is directed away from them to public programs.

industries.industry: Stock and derivatives exchanges and brokers
industries.note: They would be legally responsible for collecting and remitting the tax, adding compliance duties, but the burden is passed through to traders.
Households under the income limits get a full credit, so they are unaffected; those above the limits pay slightly more on their trades.
